summary: Proposes an experiment in subnetting a class A network address block. The goal was to find and fix software that does not handle subnetted class A addresses. It is an experimental document; results are in RFC 1879.

plainLanguage.summary: Cut a very big cake into slices to see which kitchen tools fail at slicing it. The goal was to find the computers that could not cope.

questions: what was the class a subnet experiment
how did the class a experiment use as numbers
subtitle: A temporary experiment that carved class A network 39 into small pieces to flush out buggy routing software.

tldr.problem: Some routing software in use might not handle subnetted class A addresses correctly, yet such addresses might be needed before long.
tldr.mechanism: IANA temporarily designates class A network 39 and splits the other 24 bits, either by an AS number plus a local octet or by a variable prefix, with matching DNS delegation under 39.IN-ADDR.ARPA.
tldr.outcome: The experiment was set to run from 1-May-95 to 1-Dec-95, and the addresses could be reassigned afterwards. The scheme was explicitly not a model for future allocation.

today: RFC 1797 is an Experimental document with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed. Its stated end date for the experiment was 1-Dec-95.

sections.title: Why Run the Experiment
sections.content:
There was interest in experimenting with subnetting class A addresses. The RFC says there is some evidence that not all routing software in use deals correctly with them, and that actual use of subnetted class A addresses might be necessary in the not too distant future.

So it suggests an experiment now, to identify and fix software that does not handle them properly. To do this, IANA temporarily designates the class A network number 39. The experiment begins on 1-May-95 and its current termination date is 1-Dec-95; the addresses may be reassigned to other uses afterwards.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody knew whether some computers could cope with very big address blocks cut into small pieces, so they set up a trial to find out.

sections.title: How Network 39 Is Divided
sections.content:
The high-order octet of the 4-octet IPv4 address is 39. The low-order 24 bits are used in one of two ways, chosen by their high-order bit.

Case 1: the bit is zero and the next 15 bits are the low-order 15 bits of a previously assigned Autonomous System (AS) number. The low-order octet is for local use, expected to identify a specific publicly accessible host. Tying the address to an AS number lets the experiment start quickly with no registration step. The space each AS gets equals one class C network, and the addresses are temporary.

Case 2: the bit is one and the remaining 23 bits are assigned by IANA (currently reserved for future use). The intent is to hand experimenters prefixes of differing lengths so the prefix and local-address boundary can sit at different points.

The RFC states that neither scheme is the model for how subnetted class A addresses will actually be allocated in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The big block starts with the number 39. The rest of the number is built from a network's own ID plus a last piece the network can use for its own computers.

sections.title: Examples and DNS Support
sections.content:
A provider registered as AS 690 that wants to serve popular information from local host 7 would use the address with octets 39, 2, 178 and 7. Providers are expected to put popular Web or FTP servers on such addresses to make the experiment interesting.

DNS name and address resolution should work too. For Interesting.Alter.Net at 39.2.189.7, the owner needs an A record, and a PTR record 7.189.2.39.IN-ADDR.ARPA.. That means the 189.2.39 branch of the IN-ADDR tree is delegated to Alternet. The 39.IN-ADDR.ARPA branch is delegated to IANA, managed at ISI, and participants contact that name server's administrator to get their portion delegated further.

Providers are also encouraged to swap addresses, for example AS 690 and AS 1800 trying routing holes in each other's allocations, to test whether subnetted class A addresses can be made portable. This is not meant as the model for actual use.
sections.plainLanguage: A company gets its own slice, names its computers inside it, and the phone book for names is set up to match. Companies can also trade slices to see if routers get confused.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content: The memo says only that security issues are not discussed in it. It is an Experimental protocol: it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and discussion and suggestions for improvement are requested.
sections.plainLanguage: The note does not talk about safety. It just says this is a trial, not a rule everybody has to follow.
